sources.name: Bandar Abbas nationalists
sources.text:
A large oval seal reading ملت بندرعباس (Mellat-e Bandar Abbas, “the nation of Bandar Abbas”), struck in black on mail of the Bandar Abbas nationalists, who held the town during the Minor Tyranny from 17 March to early May 1909. The nationalists were backed by Sayyid Abd al-Husayn Lari.

On 17 March 1909, under pressure from the mujtahids of Najaf and Lari, the nationalists took over the government and the custom house of Bandar Abbas and made the karguzar, the Foreign Ministry agent, governor. The Belgian customs director refused to serve them and left, and a British gunboat arrived the same day. About 1,200 armed men held the town, yet British reports say the nationalists “kept excellent order”. On 25 March they took over the Jask customs as well, and in April they agreed to lodge the customs receipts at the British consulate. Lari withdrew most of his riflemen at the beginning of May, when the governor of the Gulf Ports returned.

Sources: British India Office records, IOR/R/15/5/9 and IOR/L/PS/20/260/3.

sources.name: Persian Government
sources.text:
The Persian Government's marks fall into three periods. In 1910–1912 the constitutional government applied control marks, often reading ممیزی شد (momayezi shod, "inspected"), in the main cities of western Persia. Not all mail was opened: officials picked out particular senders and addressees, and the mark gave the inspection a legal basis. Most dated covers fall between September 1911 and February 1912, the months of Mohammad Ali Shah's attempt to regain the throne, the rising of Salar al-Dowleh in the west and the Russian ultimatum that closed the Majles on 24 December 1911.

During the First World War Persia was neutral but occupied, and the government censored mail too. CP-30 was applied at Isfahan to mail arriving from Tehran, Qazvin, Rasht, Shiraz and Hamadan between December 1916 and April 1917, and CP-22 reads "censored in Shiraz". In September 1918 the British Legation reported that it could not censor telegrams in Tehran without the Persian Government, so the Tehran censorship of these years was a Persian operation.

From 1919 to 1921, under Vosuq al-Dowleh's government and during the Jangali rising in Gilan, the Persian administration ran numbered censors. CP-38, CP-39 and CP-40 read "audited by censor number 3, 4 and 5" (Tehran, 1920–1921), and CP-42 belongs to the same series; other numbers are recorded at Rasht, Qazvin and Baku.

Sources: Mano Amarloui, "Philately ii. Postal history", and Ahmad Karimi-Hakkak, "Censorship", Encyclopaedia Iranica; India Office records IOR/L/PS/10/613; Björn Sohrne, Russo-Persian Postal Relations, pp. 96–97.

sources.name: Kazerun nationalists
sources.text:
On 17 December 1916 Nasir Diwan, the kalantar (headman) of Kazerun, drove the South Persia Rifles out of the town and imprisoned the governor. Kazerun sat on the Bushire–Shiraz road, so every letter between Shiraz and the Gulf passed through it. A British report from Shiraz says that a censorship "was placed on the Persian posts by the Khans, or as they called it, the Millat-i-Kazerun". The consul at Shiraz telegraphed on 6 January 1917: "Posts are censored by rebels at Kazerun".

The nationalists' violet oval seal, CP-27, reads "Dar Kazeroun taftish shod" ("inspected at Kazerun") and is recorded from December 1916 to January 1917. From late December 1916 they also handstamped stamps on mail passing through the town "Mellat-e Kazerun" (ملت کازرون). Mail that went on to Shiraz was read again there by the Persian censor, so some letters carry both marks.

The rebels held Kazerun until the Bushire Field Force entered the town without opposition on 27 January 1919, a few days after Nasir Diwan had left.

Sources: India Office records IOR/L/PS/10/612 and 613; F. J. Moberly, Operations in Persia 1914–1919, pp. 211–212 and 457–458; Persiphila, Kazeroun issues.

sources.name: Russian forces
sources.text:
Russian troops entered northern Persia in 1909 and stayed at Tabriz and Qazvin. In the war, General Baratoff's column occupied Hamadan by 14 December 1915 and Kermanshah in February 1916, retreated before the Ottomans in the summer of 1916, and took Hamadan again on 2 March 1917. After the revolution the Russian army in Persia broke up over the winter of 1917–1918.

When the Russian army held the west it censored all postal matter. A bilingual rectangular Russian military censor, usually black, is recorded at Hamadan in both occupations. Mossavar-Rahmani attributes CP-98 to the Russian forces; it is on mail of April to November 1917, between Hamadan, Zanjan and Isfahan.

Sources: F. J. Moberly, Operations in Persia 1914–1919, pp. 199 and 228; Björn Sohrne, Russo-Persian Postal Relations, pp. 73–75; Mano Amarloui, "Philately ii. Postal history", Encyclopaedia Iranica.

sources.name: Ottoman forces
sources.text:
Ottoman forces occupied Tabriz in January 1915, when the British Minister reported that "the Turks have put a censor in the Persian telegraph office". They took Kermanshah on 1 July and Hamadan on 10 August 1916, with Nezam al-Saltaneh's Provisional National Government at Kermanshah under their protection, and imposed strict censorship. After the British crossing of the Tigris they were ordered out of Hamadan on 23 and 26 February 1917, and the Russians entered on 2 March.

Mossavar-Rahmani attributes CP-103 to the Ottoman forces. Its only strike here is on a letter posted at Senneh for Hamadan on 26 February 1917, in the last days of the occupation. Persian mail of 1916–1917 from Kermanshah and Hamadan is also known with a Turkish rectangular censor box beside a Persian seal.

Sources: India Office records IOR/L/PS/10/479; F. J. Moberly, Operations in Persia 1914–1919, pp. 199 and 228; Military Postal History Society, Turkish occupation exhibit; Mano Amarloui, "Philately ii. Postal history", Encyclopaedia Iranica.

sources.name: British forces, south
sources.text:
From July 1915 all Persian mails from Bushire and Bandar Abbas were sent to the post office at Karachi for censorship, and on 8 August 1915 British forces occupied Bushire and replaced the Persian administration. The "Bushire under British Occupation" stamps date from that autumn. Mail that British censors opened was resealed with a printed label, "Opened under martial law"; the Force D censor's office describes a clerk who "gums the flap, closes it, and pastes on a label".

The British kept censoring civilian mail at Bushire after Persian administration returned. CP-79, the Bushire censor, is on mail between Bushire, Behbahan and Ram Hormoz from November 1916 to June 1918. Inland, the khans opposed to the British ran their own censors at Borazjan and Kazerun, so mail on the Bushire roads was often read by both sides. The Bushire Field Force reopened the road to Shiraz in January 1919.

Sources: India Office records IOR/L/PS/10/485, IOR/L/PS/10/243 and IOR/L/MIL/17/5/3230 and 3269; F. J. Moberly, Operations in Persia 1914–1919, pp. 98 and 457.

sources.name: Indian field post
sources.text:
Indian troops in Persia were served by the Indian Army's field post. Field post offices worked between Bushire and Shiraz from 1918, with the British mission escort from Bandar Abbas to Kerman and Shiraz from 1916, on the East Persia Cordon from Meshed to Dalbandin, and with Indian units of the North Persia Force at Qazvin.

Their mail was censored by the army: soldiers' letters by their own regimental officers, and all outward letters again at the base post office, where they were resealed with an "Opened under Martial Law" label. The East Persia report for 1919–1920 says that there "the system of censorship was complete". The field post offices were mostly withdrawn from April 1919.

Sources: Geoffrey Clarke, The Post Office of India and its Story (1921), chapter XVIII; India Office records IOR/L/MIL/17/5/3269 and IOR/L/MIL/17/15/35; Björn Sohrne, Russo-Persian Postal Relations, p. 95.

sources.name: British forces, north
sources.text:
From early 1918 to spring 1921 British forces held the road from Baghdad through Kermanshah, Hamadan and Qazvin to Rasht and Enzeli. General Dunsterville's mission (Dunsterforce) was formed in January 1918 to reach the Caucasus, held Baku from mid-August to mid-September 1918, and became the North Persia Force (Norperforce) under General Thomson on 16 September 1918, with headquarters at Qazvin. Norperforce garrisoned Qazvin, Hamadan, Rasht and Enzeli, fought the Jangalis in Gilan, and withdrew into Mesopotamia in spring 1921.

Both forces took political control of the west and north-west and censored the civilian Persian mail on their road. British records mention a Chief Field Censor and a British postal censor at Rasht. The marks read "Dunsterforce" (CP-84, 1918–1919) and "Passed by Censor / Norperforce", and numbered British censors such as No. 553 and No. 560 were used at Rasht and Hamadan. CP-81 to CP-97 on these covers belong to this series.

Sources: F. J. Moberly, Operations in Persia 1914–1919; India Office records IOR/L/PS/10/622 and 966; Björn Sohrne, Russo-Persian Postal Relations, pp. 92–97; FIBIS wiki, "Norperforce".

sources.name: Reza Khan’s army
sources.text:
After the coup of 21 February 1921 Tehran was put under martial law, and Reza Khan, as War Minister and from October 1923 Prime Minister, governed much of the country through military governors. British reports record a "strict postal censorship" by the Persian military authorities at Kashan from 29 August 1922, censorship of letters and telegrams at Rasht in the winter of 1922–1923, and martial law and telegram censorship after the murder of the American vice-consul Robert Imbrie in Tehran on 18 July 1924.

Town military commands stamped resealed mail "Military Censor", often with the solar year 1303 (1924–1925); examples are known from Rasht, Qazvin, Hamadan, Kermanshah, Khomein and Shiraz. CP-56 is on a letter from Tabriz to Arak of May 1924, and CP-72 on a letter from Behbahan to Shiraz of January 1925, weeks after Sheikh Khazal of Mohammerah submitted to Reza Khan's army. Military censorship continued until Reza Shah's accession.

Sources: India Office records IOR/L/PS/10/966 and 1041 and IOR/R/15/1/713; Mano Amarloui, "Philately ii. Postal history", and Ahmad Karimi-Hakkak, "Censorship", Encyclopaedia Iranica.

sources.name: Western republicans
sources.text:
In the winter of 1923–1924 Reza Khan's supporters campaigned to end the Qajar monarchy and declare a republic, against strong opposition from the clergy led by Modarres; the British Residency at Bushire reported that the campaign "suddenly fizzled out at Nauroz" 1924. Pro-republic groups took over some city administrations in western Persia and censored mail.

At Hamadan the censor used a boxed mark, 46 × 15 mm, in dark blue or black, reading سانسور جمهوری طلبان غرب ۱۳۰۳ ("Censor of the Western Republicans, 1303"). The year 1303 began on 21 March 1924, and Mossavar-Rahmani records genuine use only in April 1924, on official mail from Hamadan to Tehran and other towns.

Most surviving strikes were applied later by Mirza Massih Khan, the postal inspector (nazem des postes) at Hamadan, who kept the handstamp and used it "without discrimination", including on mail of 1922–1923 addressed to him. A study by Sasan Pejhan and IPSC members lists 79 covers and cards and 3 waybills with the mark.

Sources: Farzin Mossavar-Rahmani, Censor & Control Markings of Iran 1910–1946, pp. 90–92; India Office records IOR/R/15/1/713; Mano Amarloui, "Philately ii. Postal history", Encyclopaedia Iranica.
